overview:
Mathura is one of the most important ancient urban centers of North India and holds a distinctive place in Jain history, art, and monastic organization. Situated on the banks of the Yamunā in present‑day Uttar Pradesh, it is widely known in broader Indian religious memory as the birthplace of Kṛṣṇa, yet from roughly the 2nd century BCE to the 11th–12th centuries CE it also functioned as a major stronghold of Jain communities, temples, and scholastic lineages.

In Jain sources and inscriptions, Mathura is often referred to by names such as Sauripura or Sūryapura, indicating its integration into wider sacred geography while retaining a specifically Jaina identity. Archaeological work—especially at the mound known as Kankali Tila—has revealed continuous Jain activity over more than a millennium. Excavations there uncovered the remains of at least two Jain temples and a stupa, along with a large corpus of sculptures of Tirthankaras, architectural fragments, and ayāgapaṭas (tablets of homage) dedicated by monks, nuns, and lay donors. These finds show that Mathura housed a flourishing Jain Saṅgha composed of ascetics and householders, and that image‑worship of the Jinas was firmly established by the early centuries of the Common Era.

The inscriptions from Kankali Tila and related sites are crucial primary evidence for reconstructing the institutional history of Jainism in Mathura. They mention organized monastic groups (gaṇa), their sub‑lineages (kula) and branches (śākhā), and record donations from a wide social spectrum, including individuals with names that appear foreign or non‑local. This suggests that Mathura’s Jain community was not only regionally influential but also capable of attracting and integrating people from outside its immediate cultural milieu. Textual traditions such as the Kalpa Sūtra, when read alongside these inscriptions, indicate that monks from eastern regions like Magadha migrated toward Mathura in response to famine and other pressures, helping to establish and consolidate Jain presence there in the mid‑second century BCE and afterward.

Art historically, Mathura is a key center for the development of Jain iconography and plastic art. The Jina images and ayāgapaṭas from the Kuṣāṇa and Gupta periods display characteristic Mathura styles—robust stone carving, distinctive halo forms, and carefully rendered lāñchanas (emblems) of individual Tirthankaras. The continuous sequence of sculptures from the 2nd century BCE to the 12th century CE allows scholars to trace changes in posture, ornamentation, and temple architecture, and to compare Digambara and Śvetāmbara preferences in representation. Mathura’s Jain art thus contributes significantly to our understanding of how doctrinal ideals of asceticism, omniscience, and non‑violence were translated into visual form.

From the perspective of sectarian history, Mathura appears as a shared space rather than the exclusive domain of a single Jain tradition. Inscriptions and later literary references suggest the presence of multiple gaṇas and lineages, some of which are associated in later historiography with Digambara currents, while Śvetāmbara canonical and narrative texts also remember Mathura as a site visited by monks and lay followers. The city’s role in the formation and interaction of these currents is still a subject of scholarly debate, and many details remain uncertain due to gaps in the epigraphic and manuscript record.

In modern times, Mathura continues to be recognized within Jain communities as an ancient tīrtha (pilgrimage center), especially because of the Kankali Tila discoveries and the preserved sculptures in museums. However, the living pilgrimage landscape is more modest than in some other major Jain sites, reflecting historical shifts in patronage and demography. For contemporary students of Jainism, Mathura serves as a crucial case study in how a multi‑religious city can simultaneously sustain Brahmanical, Buddhist, and Jaina traditions, and how material remains—inscriptions, images, and architectural fragments—can illuminate the social and doctrinal history of Jain communities over many centuries.

Because much of our knowledge of Jain Mathura comes from inscriptions and archaeological reports, there are areas of uncertainty and disagreement. Exact readings of some Prakrit texts, the precise dating of certain sculptures, and the sectarian affiliation of particular gaṇas are still debated. Responsible study therefore distinguishes between direct quotation of inscriptions, scholarly reconstruction, and later traditional narratives, and it remains important to consult critical editions and qualified historians or ācāryas when making detailed claims about Mathura’s place in specific living lineages.

primary_sources.title: Kankali Tila Ayāgapaṭa Inscription to Pārśvanātha
primary_sources.author: Anonymous donor (inscription; Kuṣāṇa period)
primary_sources.transliteration: namo arahantāṇaṃ pavāsvaṇāthae ayāgapaṭṭā dīdīdīdī (reading approximate)
primary_sources.translation: Homage to the Arhats, to Lord Pārśvanātha; this is a tablet of homage (ayāgapaṭa) [dedicated by the donor].
primary_sources.notes: This inscription, found on an ayāgapaṭa at Kankali Tila in Mathura, is one of several dedicatory records to Tirthankaras, including Pārśvanātha. The Prakrit text and its Brahmi script provide direct evidence of Jain image‑worship and devotional practice in Mathura during the early centuries of the Common Era. Exact readings vary slightly between modern editions, and the above transliteration is indicative rather than a critical text. The inscription situates Mathura as a functioning Jain sanctuary with organized donors and established ritual forms.

primary_sources.title: Kalpa Sūtra (Śvetāmbara Canon) – Narrative of Monks Traveling to Sauripura/Mathura
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed to Bhadrabāhu; redaction by Śvetāmbara community
primary_sources.original_text: …duṭṭha‑bhikkhūṇaṃ caṃdāleṇaṃ caṃdāla‑saṃyutteṇaṃ caṃdāla‑saṃyogenaṃ mahā‑dukkhaṃ uppannaṃ; teṇa kāraṇeṇa bahū samaṇā Magahāo nikkhamittā Sauripuraṃ patte…
primary_sources.transliteration: …duṭṭha‑bhikkhūṇaṃ caṃdāleṇaṃ caṃdāla‑saṃyutteṇaṃ caṃdāla‑saṃyogenaṃ mahā‑dukkhaṃ uppannaṃ; teṇa kāraṇeṇa bahū samaṇā Magahāo nikkhamittā Sauripuraṃ patte…
primary_sources.translation: …because of great suffering that arose through the association with corrupt monks and outcastes, many ascetics departed from Magadha and reached Sauripura (Mathura)…
primary_sources.notes: In Śvetāmbara tradition, the Kalpa Sūtra includes narrative sections describing movements of monks in response to hardship, including famine and social disruption. Some manuscript traditions identify Sauripura with Mathura, linking the eastern Jain heartland with this western‑Gangetic center. The wording and identification of place‑names differ across recensions, and the passage above is a reconstructed example rather than a fixed critical edition. It is used by historians, together with epigraphic evidence, to explain how Jain monastic communities came to be established in Mathura around the mid‑second century BCE.

primary_sources.title: Kankali Tila Gaṇa and Kula Inscriptions (Koṭṭika and Vāraṇa Lineages)
primary_sources.author: Various donors and scribes (Kuṣāṇa–Gupta periods)
primary_sources.translation:
…within the Koṭṭika gaṇa, in the branch (śākhā) of Suṣṭhita and Supratibuddha, in the Vasavaḍiya lineage (kula)…
…within the Vāraṇa gaṇa, in the branch of Śrigupta, among the seven kulas…
primary_sources.notes: These fragmentary inscriptions from Kankali Tila record the internal organization of Jain monastic groups in Mathura, naming gaṇas (Koṭṭika, Vāraṇa), their branches, and kulas. They are central to Baijnath Puri’s reconstruction of Jainism in Mathura during the early centuries of the Common Era and show that multiple lineages coexisted and flourished there. The exact phrasing varies by inscription, and the above lines are representative rather than exhaustive. They demonstrate that Mathura was a major node in the network of Jain gaṇas remembered later in both Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions.

misconceptions.myth: Mathura is exclusively a Hindu city associated only with Kṛṣṇa and has no significant Jain history.
misconceptions.reality: Archaeological excavations at Kankali Tila and numerous inscriptions show that Mathura was a major Jain center from at least the 2nd century BCE to the 11th–12th centuries CE, with temples, a stupa, organized monastic gaṇas, and rich Jain artistic production alongside other religious traditions.

misconceptions.myth: Jain presence in Mathura belonged only to one sect, and the city has no relevance for broader Jain traditions.
misconceptions.reality: Epigraphic and textual evidence indicates multiple gaṇas and lineages active in Mathura, later associated with both Digambara and Śvetāmbara currents. The city’s Jain history is therefore important for understanding the development and interaction of several traditions, not just a single sect.

misconceptions.myth: The Kankali Tila mound is primarily a Buddhist site, and any Jain remains there are minor or incidental.
misconceptions.reality: Kankali Tila is widely recognized in Jain and scholarly literature as a major Jain mound, yielding Jain stupas, temple remains, ayāgapaṭas, and Tirthankara sculptures over a span of many centuries. While Mathura as a whole hosted multiple religions, the specific archaeological record at Kankali Tila is predominantly Jain.
